t: In a parliamentary democracy voters elect a parliament, and the government is formed from it and stays in office only as long as it keeps the confidence of a parliamentary majority.
The system grew up in Britain, where between the 1720s and the 1830s real executive power passed from the monarch to a prime minister and cabinet answerable to the House of Commons.
Spread through the British Empire and across Europe after 1918 and 1945, it is praised for flexibility and clear responsibility and blamed for unstable coalitions and weak checks on a majority.
dyk: Germany’s Basic Law lets the Bundestag remove a chancellor only by electing a successor in the same vote, a rule meant to avoid the crises of the Weimar Republic; it has succeeded once, when Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt in 1982.
ev: Robert Walpole heads the British government until 1742; he is usually counted the first prime minister
Lord North resigns in the face of the first motion of no confidence in a whole British government
The Reform Act widens the franchise and strengthens the Commons’ hold on the choice of government
Nova Scotia and the Province of Canada win responsible government, the first British colonies to do so
The Parliament Act ends the House of Lords’ absolute veto over bills passed by the House of Commons
The Reichstag passes the Enabling Act, ending parliamentary government in the Weimar Republic
West Germany’s Basic Law introduces the constructive vote of no confidence
India’s constitution makes it a parliamentary republic on the Westminster model

f.power: A prime minister and cabinet who command a majority in the elected lower house; a monarch or president serves as a largely ceremonial head of state
f.legitimacy: The election of the parliament by the voters, and the continuing confidence of its majority in the government
f.chosen: The head of state appoints whoever can command the confidence of parliament, usually the leader of the largest party or coalition; a vote of no confidence or a lost election removes the government
f.examples: Great Britain and the United Kingdom (since the 1720s), the Dominion of Canada (since 1867), the French Third Republic (1870–1940), the Weimar Republic (1919–1933), the Federal Republic of Germany (since 1949), the Republic of India (since 1950)
